newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end barely lower, data awaited.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end barely lower, data awaited.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended a quiet trading session slightly lower on Monday as most investors stepped to the sidelines to wait for economic data due later this week.
Prices moved in narrow ranges. The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond at 97-17/32, down 1/32. Its yield finished at 6.82 percent, unchanged from Friday's close.
"We ended where we started and we didn't go too far in between," said Matthew Alexy, chief markets strategist at Credit Suisse First Boston.
"It was very quiet," agreed Lee Youngdahl, bond market analyst at Aubrey G. Lanston & Co. "Nobody was doing anything."
Alexy said while there was not a lot of followthrough from Friday's short-covering, there was enough to stave off much price deterioration.

"The Beige Book, retail sales and PPI are the three things the market is waiting for," he said, referring to the Fed's anecdotal account of business conditions across the nation (due on Wednesday), February retail sales data (due Thursday) and the February Producer Price Index (PPI) (due on Friday).

The Federal Reserve's move to add permanent reserves to the banking system by buying coupons maturing between the dates of 11/15/07 and 2/15/27 provided the highlight of the session, lifting prices off their lows.
The Fed said its coupon pass totaled $1.117 billion and analysts said the reserve addition was related to a seasonal need for reserves in the banking system.
"The Fed bought a fairly large amount of coupons," said Chris Rupkey, vice president and financial economist at Bank of Tokyo/Mitsubishi.
Rupkey called it surprising that the market was not able to climb further after the coupon pass.
"They bought long bonds and the market couldn't go up on that," he said.
The Fed's purchases at the long end of the maturity range helped to flatten the yield curve, Rupkey said.
Yields were stable at the 30-year long end of the yield curve while yields on two-year maturities rose slightly.
The spread between two- and 30-year securities narrowed to 72 basis points from 74 basis points at the close on Friday.
The reason the market is anxious to see economic data due later in the week is to try to get a clearer idea of whether the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at the end of March.

February payroll data released on Friday persuaded some economists that the Fed would, indeed, raise rates at its policy meeting on March 25. But those convinced of that were still a minority, according to the most recent Reuters poll.
Regarding the chance of a Federal Reserve interest rate increase, Youngdahl said, "There's a Damocles sword hanging over us until March 25. That's not going to change."
Three-month bill rates ended down two basis points to 5.06 percent. Six-month bill rates were unchanged at 5.18 percent. Year bill rates were up two basis points to 5.38 percent.
Two-year notes were down 1/32 at 99-19/32, yielding 6.10 percent. Five-year notes were down 2/32 at 99-13/32, yielding 6.39 percent. Ten-year notes were down 1/32 to 97-27/32, yielding 6.55 percent.
